chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Portfolio Thinking Beats Stock Picking

lessons.title: Case Study: Two Nifty Stocks, One Surprising Portfolio Risk Number

children.text: You now have every tool you need to run this case study yourself: how to compute a single stock's return and risk from Lesson 2, and how to combine stocks into a portfolio return from Lesson 3. Point both at two real Nifty 50 constituents, TCS and Maruti Suzuki, and a number falls out that catches most people off guard, even people who already believe in diversification.

body.text: Combining two risky stocks can produce a portfolio that is measurably LESS risky than either stock is on its own. Not less risky than average. Less risky than the safer of the two, individually. This is not a trick. It is arithmetic, and this lesson walks through it in full.

children.text: The Setup: Six Months, Two Nifty 50 Stocks, Equal Weights

TCS and Maruti Suzuki were picked deliberately. TCS's revenue moves with global IT spending and the rupee-dollar rate. Maruti Suzuki's moves with domestic rural demand, festive-season sales, and input costs like steel and semiconductors. Different businesses, different customers, different currencies of exposure. A ₹2,00,000 book is split 50/50 between the two, and here are six months of illustrative returns for each:

body.caption: Monthly returns, TCS and Maruti Suzuki (illustrative)

children.text: Step 1: Each Stock's Own Risk, Lesson 2's Method Applied Twice
Nothing new here. Run each column through the exact mean and standard deviation formulas from Lesson 2.

content.caption: TCS: mean = 0.5%, deviations and squared deviations

children.text: Sum of squared deviations is 17.5. Variance is 17.5 / 6 = 2.92. Standard deviation is the square root of 2.92, which is 1.71%.

content.caption: Maruti Suzuki: mean = 0.5%, deviations and squared deviations

children.text: Sum of squared deviations is 23.5. Variance is 23.5 / 6 = 3.92. Standard deviation is the square root of 3.92, which is 1.98%.

Lesson 3 showed that portfolio RETURN is exactly the weighted average of individual returns. It is tempting, and wrong, to assume portfolio RISK works the same way. The naive shortcut below is what most people guess, including plenty of finance students before they have seen it proven wrong.

body.latex: \sigma_{naive} = w_1 \sigma_1 + w_2 \sigma_2 \quad \text{(WRONG for risk, unlike return)}
body.caption: The naive, incorrect shortcut: treating portfolio risk as a simple weighted average of individual risks.

body.label: Naive guess for the 50/50 portfolio's risk

children.text: Step 3: What the Portfolio Actually Did

Building the real answer needs no new formula, only the ones you already have. First, use Lesson 3's weighted-return formula to build the portfolio's own monthly return in each of the six months. Then, treat that new six-number series exactly like any single asset's returns, and run it through Lesson 2's mean and standard deviation formulas.

body.caption: Portfolio return each month (50% TCS + 50% Maruti Suzuki)

body.title: Monthly returns: TCS, Maruti Suzuki, and the 50/50 portfolio

children.text: Look at the chart before reading further. The portfolio line, in every single month, sits between the two stock lines, and its swings are visibly smaller than either individual line's swings. That visual is the whole lesson, before you even compute a single number.

The six portfolio returns sum to 3.0%, giving a mean of 0.5%, exactly what Lesson 3's formula predicts: 0.5 x 0.5% + 0.5 x 0.5%. The squared deviations from that mean sum to 13.5. Variance is 13.5 / 6 = 2.25. Standard deviation is the square root of 2.25, which is exactly 1.5%.

body.text: Read that statGrid again. The portfolio's standard deviation, 1.50%, is not just below the naive guess of 1.84%. It is below TCS's own standalone risk of 1.71%, and well below Maruti Suzuki's 1.98%. Owning both stocks together is less risky than owning only the safer of the two, alone. Nobody removed risk by magic. The two stocks' bad months and good months landed in different calendar months often enough to partially cancel out in the combined series.

children.text: Look back at the return table. In Month 2, TCS fell while Maruti Suzuki rose. In Month 5, TCS rose while Maruti Suzuki fell. These two stocks did not move in lockstep across the six months, which is exactly the correlation idea introduced in Lesson 1. On this small sample, TCS and Maruti Suzuki moved together only loosely, a correlation of roughly 0.32, low enough for real cancellation to occur, but nowhere close to the -1 that would be needed to eliminate risk entirely.

body.text: This lesson found 1.50% only by building the entire portfolio return series by hand, month by month, and running it back through Lesson 2's formula. That works, but it is slow, and it required six months of paired data before the number existed at all. Chapter 2 gives you a single formula, built from each stock's variance plus their covariance, that predicts this same 1.50% directly from the two stocks' individual risk numbers and their correlation, without ever constructing the combined series.

body.title: Compute the naive guess
body.prompt: Two stocks have monthly standard deviations of 4% and 6%. An investor builds an equal-weighted (50/50) portfolio. What is the NAIVE weighted-average guess for the portfolio's standard deviation, using the (incorrect) shortcut from Step 2 of this lesson?
body.explanation: Naive guess = (0.5 x 4%) + (0.5 x 6%) = 2% + 3% = 5%. As this lesson showed, the true portfolio standard deviation will almost always be lower than this naive guess, unless the two stocks are perfectly positively correlated, the one case Chapter 2 covers where the naive shortcut and the truth actually agree.

body.title: What exactly was surprising here
body.question: In this lesson's case study, the actual 50/50 portfolio's standard deviation (1.50%) turned out to be lower than which of the following?
options: Only Maruti Suzuki's own standard deviation (1.98%)
Both the naive guess AND both individual stocks' own standard deviations
Nothing, 1.50% was actually the highest of the numbers computed in this lesson
body.explanation: 1.50% is lower than the naive guess (1.84%), lower than TCS's own risk (1.71%), and lower than Maruti Suzuki's own risk (1.98%). The portfolio is safer than either half of it held alone, which is the genuinely surprising result this lesson set out to demonstrate.

body.title: Explain it to a skeptical friend
body.scenario: A friend says: "I don't get how adding a second stock can make my portfolio LESS risky than the safer stock I already owned. Doesn't adding any second holding always add some risk?"
body.prompt: Using this lesson's TCS and Maruti Suzuki numbers, how would you explain what actually happened, in plain terms?
body.modelAnswer: Adding a second holding does not automatically add risk if that holding does not move in lockstep with what you already own. TCS and Maruti Suzuki's monthly returns moved together only loosely (correlation around 0.32), so TCS's bad months (like Month 2) were often offset by a good month for Maruti Suzuki, and vice versa in Month 5. Averaging their returns together each month smoothed out swings that would have hit a single-stock holder in full. The portfolio was not risk-free, its return still moved from -2.5% to +2.0% across the six months, but its overall variability was smaller than either stock's on its own, precisely because the two stocks' ups and downs did not line up on the same months.

cards.definition: The incorrect assumption that portfolio standard deviation equals the weighted average of individual stocks' standard deviations. True only when correlation equals exactly 1.
The gap between the naive weighted-average guess for portfolio risk and the portfolio's true, lower standard deviation.
The result, possible whenever correlation is meaningfully below 1, where a portfolio's risk is lower than either of its individual holdings' own risk.

points: Building a portfolio's actual risk number requires nothing new: apply Lesson 3's weighted-return formula month by month, then apply Lesson 2's mean and standard deviation formulas to that new combined series.
The naive shortcut, weighting each stock's individual risk by its portfolio weight, is WRONG for risk, even though the equivalent shortcut is exactly correct for return.
In this case study, the true portfolio standard deviation (1.50%) came in below the naive guess (1.84%), and below BOTH individual stocks' own standard deviations (1.71% and 1.98%).
This happens because the two stocks' good and bad months did not consistently line up together, a correlation loose enough (around 0.32 here) for real cancellation.
The naive shortcut only becomes correct in the special case where two assets are perfectly positively correlated, meaning correlation equals exactly 1.
Chapter 2 replaces this lesson's slow, by-hand method with a single formula that predicts the portfolio's risk directly from each stock's variance and their covariance, no combined series required.
